To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relative dominance of two competing parasitoids of a shared prey species is determined by productivity of the prey.

(1) Aphytis and Encarsia are the dominant parasitoids of California red scale in all three cultivar types; (2) Encarsia dominates in orange and grapefruit, whereas Aphytis dominates in lemon; (3) the relative abundance of Aphytis is positively related to scale productivity; (4) the relative abundance and the total density of scale is positively related to the dominance of Aphytus.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IG predator is a keystone species in this system, as its dominance shifts the system from one in which the prey species is the keystone to one where the IG predator is.

The main takeaway from our work is that
IGP theory is a useful framework for predicting the dynamics of species interactions in the field, even in complex food webs.
IGP can be an important structuring force in communities.
intraguild predations can be a key mechanism for regulating the dynamics of food webs, and that the strength of intraguild predators can shift along gradients in resource productivity.
